column1: # Trigger fixtures — realistic user phrasings and the skill that should fire.
# Format: <prompt><TAB><expected-skill>[,<also-acceptable-skill>...]
# Rules for adding a row:
#   - Write how a user actually talks, not the skill's own vocabulary. A prompt that
#     quotes the description tests nothing.
#   - Never name the skill in the prompt. That measures obedience, not routing.
#   - Three phrasings per skill minimum: one obvious, one oblique, one where the user
#     jumps straight to the work and the skill has to fire unprompted.
#   - A row that always passes is dead weight; a row that always fails is the finding.
#   - Opt-in skills (their descriptions say "do not auto-trigger") legitimately return
#     NONE on an indirect ask. List both — `skill,NONE` — so the row records the real
#     contract instead of failing the skill for obeying it.
# A miss is not automatically a skill defect. Decide which it is before editing:
# either the description is missing a trigger phrase, or the fixture is wrong about
# what should happen. Changing the skill to satisfy a bad fixture is how a suite starts
# lying to you.
# Two rows below list several skills because the prompt is genuinely ambiguous and more
# than one answer is right: "how would i even know if this worked" is both a success-check
# question and a measurement question; "it works but only about half the time" is both a
# flakiness problem and a debugging problem. Those rows record a real boundary between
# skills rather than pretending one answer is correct — an eval that forces a single
# answer onto an ambiguous prompt measures the fixture author, not the kit.
